podcast.title: Death Details - August 13, 2024
podcast.body: Greg Kihn died on August 13, 2024, at the age of 75, due to complications from Alzheimer's disease. "It finally caught up to him on August 13, 2024. He was 75."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alzheimer's Diagnosis
podcast.body: Unbeknownst to the public at the time of his 2018 retirement from radio, Greg Kihn was suffering from Alzheimer's disease. "What we didn't know at the time was that he was suffering from Alzheimer's."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Authorial Career
podcast.body: Beyond music, Greg Kihn was also a published author, having written six novels and numerous short stories. "He wrote six novels and a bunch of short stories."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Categorization in the 1980s
podcast.body: Greg Kihn was, for a time in the early 1980s, included in the early mix of alternative or new wave artists, often under the Powerpop umbrella. This categorization stemmed from the prevailing trend of labeling any short, sharp rock songs as Powerpop, which blurred genre lines. "But by the time we got to the middle of the decade, big guitar sounds with big hooks that just happened to have pot melodies were coming back into Vogue, thanks to groups like REM."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hobby - Breeding Praying Mantises
podcast.body: For leisure, Greg Kihn pursued the unusual hobby of breeding rare praying mantises. "and for fun, he bred rare praying mantises."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Radio DJ Career
podcast.body: After his musical career, Greg Kihn transitioned into working as a radio DJ in San Jose, California, a role he held until his retirement in 2018. "Greg later transitioned into a job as a radio DJ in San Jose, California, and for fun, he bred rare praying mantises. The DJ gig lasted until 2018 when he announced his retirement."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Categorization in the 1980s
xref.body: Rick Springfield, like Tom Petty and Greg Kihn, was occasionally grouped into the early alternative, new wave, or Powerpop categories in the early 1980s. This classification was a result of the broad tendency to label any succinct, energetic rock song as Powerpop during a period of genre fluidity. "This happened due to a tendency at the time to categorize all short, sharp rock songs as PowerPop. And if they were PowerPop, then they were New Wave, right?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Opening for The Rolling Stones
xref.body: During their peak, The Greg Kihn Band earned the opportunity to open for The Rolling Stones. "and a chance to open for the Rolling Stones."
